# 2024 Women's T20 World Cup

The **2024 Women's T20 World Cup** was the ninth edition of the [Women's T20 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_T20_World_Cup "Women's T20 World Cup"). Originally scheduled to be hosted in [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh") from 3 to 20 October 2024, it was later relocated to the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates") for the same dates due to political unrest in Bangladesh, although the [Bangladesh Cricket Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Cricket_Board "Bangladesh Cricket Board") still held the hosting rights.[[1]](#cite_note-Host-1) New Zealand won their first title, defeating South Africa by 32 runs in the final at Dubai.

## Contents

## Background

The [ICC Women's T20 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICC_Women's_T20_World_Cup "ICC Women's T20 World Cup") is a professional [WT20I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Twenty20_International "Women's Twenty20 International") tournament featuring women's national cricket teams, organized by the [International Cricket Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Cricket_Council "International Cricket Council") (ICC). The tournament, now being held every two years, was first played in 2009 in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England").[[7]](#cite_note-process-7) The last tournament held in 2023 in [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") was contested by 10 teams. The defending champions were [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_women's_national_cricket_team "Australia women's national cricket team"), who defeated [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa_women's_national_cricket_team "South Africa women's national cricket team") in the final of the [previous edition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_ICC_Women's_T20_World_Cup "2023 ICC Women's T20 World Cup").[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)

### Host selection

In July 2022, the ICC announced that the 2024 Women's T20 World Cup would be played in Bangladesh.[[10]](#cite_note-10) In August 2024, the ICC announced that the 2024 Women's T20 World Cup would be played in the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates"), with the [Bangladesh Cricket Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_Cricket_Board "Bangladesh Cricket Board") remaining the official hosts.[[1]](#cite_note-Host-1)[[11]](#cite_note-UAE-11)

### Format

The 10 qualifying teams were divided into [two groups of five teams](#Group_stage); all the five teams in a group played with all the others – for a total of ten matches – and the top two teams in each group advanced to the [knockout stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_ICC_Men's_T20_World_Cup_knockout_stage "2024 ICC Men's T20 World Cup knockout stage").[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14)

### Schedule

On 28 July 2024, ICC announced that the tournament will be played from 3 to 20 October 2024.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] It was scheduled to be hosted in [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh"). However, it was later relocated to the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates") for the same dates in August 2024.[[11]](#cite_note-UAE-11) On 16 August 2024, ICC announced that warm-up fixtures will be held from 27 September to 1 October.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] However, on 27 August 2024, after the announcement of the revised schedule, the warm-up fixtures were scheduled to be held from 28 September to 1 October.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

### Prize money

The ICC allocated a pool of US$7,958,080 in prize money for the tournament. The winners would earn at least $2.34 million. In addition, each team will receive an additional $31,154 for each match they win excluding the semi-finals and final.[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)

## Qualification

In April 2022, the ICC confirmed the qualification process for the tournament. The hosts, [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh_women's_national_cricket_team "Bangladesh women's national cricket team") along with the top six teams from the [2023 tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_ICC_Women's_T20_World_Cup "2023 ICC Women's T20 World Cup") qualified automatically for the tournament. The remaining automatic qualification spot was taken by the best-ranked team in the [ICC Women's T20I Team Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICC_Women's_T20I_Team_Rankings "ICC Women's T20I Team Rankings") which had not already qualified, as of 27 February 2023.[[7]](#cite_note-process-7) The two remaining places were filled via the global qualifier, in which teams advanced from the regional qualifiers competed for it.

[Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland_women's_national_cricket_team "Scotland women's national cricket team") qualified for the Women's T20 World Cup for the first time after defeating [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland_women's_cricket_team "Ireland women's cricket team") in the first semi-final of the qualifier.[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19) [Sri Lanka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Lanka_women's_national_cricket_team "Sri Lanka women's national cricket team") became the second qualifier and reached their ninth T20 World Cup after defeating United Arab Emirates in the second semi-final.[[20]](#cite_note-20) Overall, nine out of ten teams from [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_ICC_Women's_T20_World_Cup "2023 ICC Women's T20 World Cup") reached the T20 World Cup, with the only difference being Scotland replacing [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland_women's_cricket_team "Ireland women's cricket team").[[21]](#cite_note-21)

The **2024 ICC Women's T20 World Cup final** was a [Women's Twenty20 International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Twenty20_International "Women's Twenty20 International") [cricket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cricket "Cricket") match that was played at the [Dubai International Cricket Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai_International_Cricket_Stadium "Dubai International Cricket Stadium") in [Dubai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai "Dubai"), [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates") on 20 October 2024 to determine the winner of the [2024 ICC Women's T20 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_ICC_Women's_T20_World_Cup "2024 ICC Women's T20 World Cup").[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) It was played between [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_women's_national_cricket_team "New Zealand women's national cricket team") and [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa_women's_national_cricket_team "South Africa women's national cricket team").[[3]](#cite_note-final-3)

New Zealand defeated South Africa by 32 runs to win their maiden T20 World Cup title.[[4]](#cite_note-4) [Amelia Kerr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amelia_Kerr "Amelia Kerr") was named as the Player of the Match for her all round performance of 43 (38) and 3/24 as well as the Player of the Tournament for taking 15 wickets and scoring 135 runs.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)

In August 2024, after relocating the ICC Women's T20 World Cup from [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh") to the [United Arab Emirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Arab_Emirates "United Arab Emirates"), the ICC announced that [Dubai International Cricket Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai_International_Cricket_Stadium "Dubai International Cricket Stadium"), [Dubai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai "Dubai") will be hosting the final on 20 October.[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8)

South Africa qualified for their second consecutive final losing the [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_ICC_Women's_T20_World_Cup#Final "2023 ICC Women's T20 World Cup") to Australia.[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) New Zealand on the other hand reached their third final, having lost on both previous occasions, to England in [2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_ICC_Women's_World_Twenty20#Final "2009 ICC Women's World Twenty20") and to Australia in [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_ICC_Women's_World_Twenty20#Final "2010 ICC Women's World Twenty20").[[11]](#cite_note-11) Previously, the teams have played each other five times in ICC Women's T20 World Cup with South Africa winning twice (2014, 2023) and New Zealand winning thrice (2009, 2012, 2016).[[12]](#cite_note-12) This will also be the first time that either of the teams has won the ICC Men's or Women's T20 World Cup trophy.[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)

# Women's T20 World Cup winners: Australian cricket team's dominance unmatched - full list

England and West Indies have been T20 world champions too. The Indian women's cricket team finished runners-up once. Full list of Women's T20 World Cup winners.

Picture by 2026 Getty Images

By Ali Asgar Nalwala

[**T20**](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/first-t20-cricket-match) has helped [**women's cricket**](https://olympics.com/en/news/women-t20-cricket-records-international) grow by leaps and bounds over the last few years. Despite this expansion, the dominance of Australia in the **Women's T20 World Cup** remains unchallenged.

First played in 2009, 10 editions of the Women's T20 World Cup have been held so far. Australia emerged as world champions on seven occasions while New Zealand, England and the West Indies complete the list of **Women's T20 World Cup winners**.

India, New Zealand and South Africa have stood as runners-up in different editions.

In what was an eight-team inaugural edition in 2009, hosts England edged out New Zealand to clinch the first-ever ICC Women's T20 World Cup title at the iconic Lord's Cricket Ground in London. Both [**cricket**](https://olympics.com/en/news/why-cricket-olympics-1900-paris-games-commonwealth-athletes-cricketers) teams emerged unbeaten from the group stages and beat Australia en route to the final.

Picture by Getty Images

England's Charlotte Edwards lifts the trophy as her team celebrates after winning the 2009 ICC Women's T20 World Cup.

[Women’s Cricket World Cup: Roll of champions

4 min read](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/women-cricket-world-cup-winners-list)

New Zealand produced exceptional batting performances throughout the inaugural edition but were bundled out for just 85 in the final. England chased down the total with six wickets and three overs to spare. England’s Claire Taylor was named the Player of the Tournament.

## **Women’s T20 World Cup winners list**

### Women’s T20 World Cup winners

| Year | Winner | Runners-up | Hosts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2009 | England | New Zealand | England |
| 2010 | Australia | New Zealand | West Indies |
| 2012 | Australia | England | Sri Lanka |
| 2014 | Australia | England | Bangladesh |
| 2016 | West Indies | Australia | India |
| 2018 | Australia | England | West Indies |
| 2020 | Australia | India | Australia |
| 2023 | Australia | South Africa | South Africa |
| 2024 | New Zealand | South Africa | UAE |
| 2026 | Australia | England | England |

The Women's T20 World Cup, mostly held biennially, has been dominated by Australia since then. The team from Down Under has made eight finals, winning seven and losing just once in 2016 against the West Indies.

New Zealand were also the team to beat in the 2010 edition held in the West Indies. The White Ferns emerged unbeaten from the group stage with convincing wins and beat the hosts by 56 runs in the semi-finals. Ultimately, Australia won the title due to their ability to handle pressure better. They registered a Super Over win against England in the group stages, beat India by four runs in the semi-final and won the final by three runs after putting up just 106 on the scoreboard.

Australia won the 2012 edition in Sri Lanka with a narrow four-run victory over rivals England in the final. After putting up a challenging 142/4 on board, a collective bowling effort led by Jess Jonassen's three-wicket haul helped Australia become the first team in the history of women's T20 to defend its World Cup title.

With the T20 gaining popularity and the quality of the teams on the rise, the ICC made the Women's T20 World Cup a 10-team affair 2014 edition onwards.

South Africa, India and the West Indies started to challenge the likes of New Zealand, England and Australia. However, Australia became the first country to win a hat-trick of T20 World Cup titles across men's and women's events with a six-wicket victory over England in the 2014 final in Mirpur.

Picture by Getty Images

Captain Meg Lanning and the Australian team celebrate after winning the 2014 ICC Women's T20 World Cup.

West Indies broke Australia's title-winning streak in 2016. Batting first once again, the defending champions posted a competitive 148/5 in the final at Eden Gardens. However, West Indian opener Hayley Matthews got the hosts off to a flyer.

Matthews struck 66 off 45 and put on 120 for the opening wicket alongside captain Stafanie Taylor. The partnership helped West Indies win the match by eight wickets. It was the first ICC trophy for the senior West Indies women's cricket team.

Picture by Getty Images

West Indies with the trophy after winning the 2016 ICC Women's T20 World Cup.

Australia came back to winning ways by lifting the trophy back in the 2018 edition hosted by the West Indies. Similar to the 2014 edition in Bangladesh, Australia bundled out England for 105 and won the match by eight wickets in 15.1 overs. Australian great Alyssa Healy finished the tournament as the leading run-getter and was also named as the player of the tournament.

India, with the likes of [Smriti Mandhana](https://olympics.com/en/news/who-is-smriti-mandhana-india-women-cricket-team), Jemimah Rodrigues and Harmanpreet Kaur in its ranks, made it to their maiden final after the semi-final against England was washed out in the 2020 edition held in Australia.

India had beaten Australia in the group stages and had topped the group. However, the final was played in front of a boisterous crowd at the MCG and Australia strolled to their fifth World Cup title with an 85-run victory over India.

Picture by Getty Images

Meg Lanning leads the celebration with the Australian cricket team after winning the 2020 ICC Women's T20 Cricket World Cup.

The 2023 edition saw hosts South Africa and Australia make the final with narrow victories in the semi-finals over England and India, respectively. However, the final result remained the same with Australia completing their second hat-trick of titles with a 19-run victory.

South African hearts were broken yet again in the Women's T20 World Cup 2024 played in the UAE. New Zealand emerged as the fourth Women's T20 World Champions in history after beating South Africa by 32 runs in the final. Australia had exited the tournament in the semi-finals.

Australia, however, bounced back to seal their seventh Women's T20 World Cup title in 2026 under captain Sophie Molineux after beating England in the final by six wickets at Lord's. They went through the group stages unbeaten, beating India and South Africa en route, before toppling the West Indies in the semi-finals.
